## KernelSeal v1.2.0

The binary name in a request is a claim, not an identity. Until now it was also
the only thing authorization rested on. This release authorizes on the caller's
cgroup instead, which the kernel sets when the container is created and which a
process cannot change from inside it.

### The problem

Any process that could open the socket could request the secrets bound to any
configured binary by naming it. No subterfuge was required: the request is a JSON
object containing a string, so a compromised container did not need to install the
binary, rename anything, or execute anything.

```bash
echo '{"binary":"/usr/bin/node"}' | nc -U /run/kernelseal/kernelseal.sock
```

On a node-wide DaemonSet, whose socket is a `hostPath` that every pod can mount,
that was cross-tenant secret disclosure. On a dedicated node it was self-only and
harmless, which is why the sidecar pattern was the documented answer.

### What changed

The agent reads the calling PID's cgroup from procfs, parses the pod UID out of
the path, and looks it up against the pods scheduled on its own node. Bindings
select on that pod:

```yaml
secrets:
  - name: checkout-db
    selector:
      binary: node            # Narrows which of this pod's bindings apply
      namespace: payments     # Authorizes: derived from the caller's cgroup
      labels:
        app: checkout
```

The `nc` command above now fails on a node-wide agent. `nc` runs in some pod's
cgroup, that pod does not match the selector, and the request is refused and
audited whatever it calls itself.

`namespace`, `labels`, `container` and `cgroupPath` were accepted by the config
parser and ignored when matching. They now decide who a binding applies to.

### policy.podIdentity

How strictly this applies depends on who can reach the socket, which is a
deployment question rather than a preference:

| Mode | Behavior | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `required` | Refuses callers it cannot attribute to a pod, and rejects bindings that name no pod | A node-wide DaemonSet |
| `preferred` (default) | Enforces pod selectors when present; still serves bindings that have none | A per-pod sidecar |
| `disabled` | Does not identify callers at all | The v1.1.0 behavior |

`deploy/manifests/daemonset.yaml` now ships `required`. The sidecar template ships
`preferred`, because its socket lives on an `emptyDir` reachable only from inside
one pod, so reaching it already proves which pod is asking.

An unrecognized value is treated as `required`. A typo in the setting that governs
authorization must not quietly widen it.

In `required` mode the agent refuses to start if it cannot watch pods. An agent
that refuses every request is more useful as a startup failure than as a pod that
looks healthy while nothing it guards can start.

### A binding that cannot be served is not dropped

Under `podIdentity: required` a binding whose selector names only a binary is
rejected at load. It is kept in the registry and marked, not discarded, so requests
for it are refused loudly:

```
[REGISTER] binding "myapp" REJECTED: policy.podIdentity is required, but this
           selector names no pod; add namespace, labels, container or cgroupPath
```

Dropping it would make the binary look unconfigured, and an unconfigured binary
starts unprotected without complaint. That would turn a configuration mistake into
a silent loss of the guarantee the agent exists to provide, which is the same
failure mode the unresolved-secret bookkeeping already guards against.

### Denials name the workload

```
[DENY] Refusing "node" to pid=6001: no binding admits this caller;
       refused [checkout-db (namespace)] (pid=6001 uid=1000 ... pod=sandbox/scratch-xyz)
```

A PID alone is close to useless on a busy node, where the process is usually gone
by the time anyone reads the log. Denials now carry the calling pod's namespace,
name and UID, and name the constraint that failed.

Refusing a caller on identity does not depend on `policy.mode`. Audit mode weakens
what the kernel blocks; it does not make one pod's secrets available to another.

### No client-go

The pod watcher is a list-watch written against the API server directly, restricted
to the agent's own node with a `spec.nodeName` field selector. client-go would have
added tens of megabytes of dependencies to a binary whose whole purpose is to be a
small static thing that loads BPF. `go.mod` gains one direct dependency,
`golang.org/x/sys`, which was already in the module graph.

The RBAC this needs, `pods: get/list/watch`, was granted in v1.0.0 and unused until
now.

### Cgroup namespaces

The kernel renders `/proc/<pid>/cgroup` relative to the *reading* process's cgroup
namespace, so an agent in its own namespace sees other pods anchored to itself:

```
0::/../docker-7f2a660030ce....scope      # agent in its own cgroup namespace
0::/system.slice/docker-7f2a....scope    # agent in the host's
```

Pod attribution is unaffected: the pod UID is parsed from a path segment, not from
the path as a whole, so `namespace`, `labels` and `container` selectors work in
both cases. Only `cgroupPath` is affected, and it refuses rather than comparing
paths anchored differently, because a coincidental match would authorize the wrong
cgroup. The agent detects this at startup and says so.

Prefer `namespace` and `labels`. `cgroupPath` is for agents running in the host's
cgroup namespace.

### Verification status

Cgroup-to-pod attribution is covered by unit tests over recorded path shapes for
the systemd and cgroupfs drivers with containerd, CRI-O and Docker, including
guaranteed-QoS pods with no QoS segment, non-default kubelet cgroup roots, cgroup
v1 hosts, and paths that must not be mistaken for pods.

**It has not yet been exercised on a live EKS node.** The path shapes are recorded
from real nodes but the end-to-end behavior on AL2023 with the systemd driver is
unverified. If you run a node-wide agent, roll it out to one node first and watch
for `no binding admits this caller` from workloads that should be authorized.

### Upgrade

Existing configurations keep working. The default `preferred` mode serves
binary-only bindings exactly as v1.1.0 did.

If you deploy the DaemonSet, it now sets `podIdentity: required` and every binding
needs a pod selector:

```yaml
selector:
  binary: myapp
  namespace: production   # add this
```

Without it the binding is rejected at load and its workload will not start. The
rejection is logged with the binding name.

```bash
ghcr.io/phonginreallife/kernelseal:v1.2.0
```
